title: Direct effects of climate and food on organisms are small

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Direct effects of climate and food on organisms are small

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The direct effect of differences in climate, food and similar conditions on an organism's structure is very small in animals and perhaps somewhat larger in plants, and cannot account for the complex co-adaptations between organisms.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: How much direct effect difference of climate, food, etc., produces on any being is extremely doubtful. My impression is, that the effect is extremely small in the case of animals, but perhaps rather more in that of plants.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter V, “Laws of Variation”; section “Effects of external conditions.”. Scope: plants and animals in nature

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch05-02: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Controlled datasets can quantify direct environmental effects and compare kingdoms. A universal magnitude claim and the separate assertion about complex co-adaptation cannot be cleanly resolved with current pooled data.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Meta-analyse common-garden and reciprocal-transplant estimates of structural plasticity caused by climate and diet, comparing plants and animals. Small average effects in animals and larger effects in plants support the claim, while large direct animal effects refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Plasticity, developmental effects and inherited adaptation are often conflated.

'Extremely small' lacks a prespecified effect-size threshold.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The direct-effect claim needs reaction norms, which exist as many experiments and not as one open database. Climate and trait repositories support only the correlative pattern, which does not isolate the effect of conditions on a given organism. A compiled subset of common gardens could compare animals and plants, with months of harmonization and incomplete taxonomic reach.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Separate direct environmental effects from genetic differences with common-garden or reciprocal-transplant reaction norms, in animals and plants, and compare the size of those plastic effects with the complexity of matched multi-species adaptations. Small animal reaction norms, somewhat larger plant norms, and plastic effects too small to build the coadaptations, would confirm the claim; plastic effects as large as genetic divergence in the same structures would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Trait-climate correlations mix plasticity, local adaptation, and biogeographic sorting.

Common-garden results are scattered in papers and are the actual measurement of direct effect.

Complex coadaptation has no single scalar in these databases.
